  [Quoting @GeniesLoki: @visakanv I think this is definitely a "Why not both?" situation (alternating not simultaneous). 1230083333981442053 [2020-02-19] @GeniesLoki 💜 1
@visakanv I agree. And for most people "produce hundreds of things" is absolutely the right advice that they should follow. But consider:

1. You personally will get better bang if you optimise bang for buck.
2. Optimising for bang for buck *is* optimising for bang.

Very different claims!

1230083994022240256 [2020-02-19] @GeniesLoki 💜 1
@visakanv Every strategy is good at different things. "Do the hard thing" will teach you very different things from "Do lots of easy things". The latter is a good strategy for unfamiliar territory, but it plateaus, and is usefully alternated with the former to break new ground.

1. Do it 100 times. 

Write 100 songs, cook 100 omelettes, talk to 100 people. It never seems like a huge deal until you try it yourself. It’s manageable, and yet it stretches you, and you’ll be observably different at the end of it. Effective way to get a foothold on a new thing
├── 1330986026848849920 [2020-11-23] @visakanv 💜 530 🔁 35
│   2. Play long games. 
│   
│   This is kind of a remix of 1. Thousands of people will want to start a substack or podcast. Something like 1% of them or less will stick with it consistently for 2 years. If you commit to things for 10+ years, you develop what appear to be superpowers
│   ↓
│   1330986630098743296 [2020-11-23] @visakanv 💜 469 🔁 28
│   3. Practice good reply game.
│   
│   Life is multiplayer co-op. You can achieve much more with others than you can by yourself. You can build relationships simply by doing good replies over a sustained period of time. Do 100 good replies over 2 years 😜 Don’t be pushy or needy about it
│   ↓
│   1330987366715064321 [2020-11-23] @visakanv 💜 518 🔁 44
│   4. Cultivate your taste.
│   
│   Everything beautiful in the world is made by people with discernment, who know what they like and why they like it, who are motivated by something deeper than just money or status. 
│   
│   This takes a while. Evaluate 100 things you love, articulate why/how
│   ↓
│   1330988588532527104 [2020-11-23] @visakanv 💜 323 🔁 19
│   5. Haters are fans too.
│   
│   Be mindful of how you spend your time and energy. 90% of the time spent complaining about what you don’t like is better spent focusing on what you do like. Don’t incentivize what you dislike. A common enemy doesn’t actually create lasting friendship
│   ↓
│   1330989616199962624 [2020-11-23] @visakanv 💜 493 🔁 67
│   6. You cannot bully people into becoming better people, because what they learn from it is that bullying is how things get done.
│   ↓
│   1330990475583442944 [2020-11-23] @visakanv 💜 510 🔁 56
│   7. The meaning of life is friends. 
│   
│   We’re here to take care of each other. We’re all walking each other home. You can come up with more grandiose versions of this - justice, liberty, happiness... it all makes more sense through the frame of human kinship.
│   ↓
│   1330991041705431040 [2020-11-23] @visakanv 💜 296 🔁 13
│   8. Narcissism is a bug of the mind. 
│   
│   It’s an optical-temporal illusion, a fixation on the narrow image of a self that doesn’t actually exist. Call it ego if you like. It’s mistaking the menu for the meal, the map for the territory. There is no self, we are all waves in the ocean
│   ↓
│   1330991780196618245 [2020-11-23] @visakanv 💜 287 🔁 18

│   ├── 1330992265016213504 [2020-11-23] @visakanv 💜 292 🔁 26
│   │   10. The public is insufficiently educated on how to be a good public.
│   │   
│   │   You could say that this is the central problem of our species. There are lots of parts to this wicked problem. There’s room for everyone to pitch in and contribute to this infinite endeavor.

1331068602951208962 [2020-11-24] @visakanv 💜 78 🔁 6
92. It’s conflict all the way up and it’s conflict all the way down. It can be helpful to list out all of the conflicts you’re currently entangled in. Once you’ve got it on paper, you start seeing all sorts of alt solutions you might not have considered when in the thick of it

93. This doesn’t generalize universally but: be careful about punishing failure, both in yourself and in others. It can incentivize  not-even-trying. 

Where possible, try rewarding attempts to learn from failure. Gentle curiosity can pull you out of a slump where anger fails

title: Visa’s “Do 100 Things” became everyone’s cheat code
summary:
Visa (@visakanv) kicked off a mini-movement by insisting that the fastest path to “10x good” work is just… shipping a ton of attempts, because your taste and standards are still forming. The trigger was a tiny beef with GeniesLoki: Loki argued impact is nonlinear so you should “optimize bang for buck,” and Visa basically said most people aren’t overproducing junk—they’re producing *nothing* because perfectionism has them in a headlock. The line that stuck was his clarification: “do 100 things” doesn’t mean easy reps, it means “things at the edge of your comfort zone.”

Peak “oh damn this is real” moment came when Visa turned it into lore with examples: the latte art story (h/t @shrinetothevine) where the first ~20 are “brown gloop” and then #30 suddenly works, plus Visa’s blunt diagnosis that the bottleneck isn’t technique—it’s emotional stamina: “the willingness to cheerfully persist through failure.” People started posting receipts: @IaimforGOAT tied it to gym attendance for 100 days and dropped 12.25kg; @AskYatharth reframed it as “5–7 gets you unblocked, 50–100 makes you invested”; @QiaochuYuan said “do 1% thing” was even more generative in scary contexts (baby-step the task until you can actually start). Visa kept re-injecting it everywhere—telling Malcolm Ocean to “do 100 appliance rants,” telling people who couldn’t pick a 100-thing to just do 100 random disjointed experiments and follow the “desire paths.”

Outcome/current state: it stopped being a single productivity tip and became a community boundary object—Threadapalooza’s 100-tweet threads, blisstweeting treating it like an “agency” practice, Visa folding it into his project-management/“flow zone” model, and even Tucker Peck mapping “50–100 repetitions” onto trauma therapy conversations. What survives is the meme-vocabulary (“do 100 thing,” “1% thing,” “5–7 to unblock”) and the permission slip: you’re not trying to be good *today*, you’re trying to be the kind of person who can keep going long enough to get good—whether that’s art, lifting, writing, or having the same hard conversation for the 80th time.
